personality_voice.book_baseline: Dumbledore in CoS is calm, authoritative, and gently wise. His voice is measured and deliberate — he asks rather than tells ('I must ask you, Harry, whether there is anything you'd like to tell me'), uses mild irony ('Impaled upon your own sword, Gilderoy'), deflects confrontation with apparent lightness ('there's a delicious-looking custard tart I want to sample'), and speaks moral truths simply and directly ('It is our choices, Harry, that show what we truly are'). He carries quiet gravity in crisis (chamber is open, suspension scene) but also warmth and even playfulness around Harry (Fawkes Burning Day, jokes about Lockhart). He is observant and penetrating — giving Harry X-ray stares, asking open questions he already knows the answer to, and staying multiple steps ahead of everyone in the room. Crucially, he controls scenes through calm precision rather than force.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves almost all of this. Dumbledore's measured cadence, his ironic aside about the custard tart, his warm amusement at Fawkes's Burning Day, his penetrating questions to Harry, his quiet steel with Lucius Malfoy, and his key moral speech ('It's not our abilities... it's our choices') are all present and tonally faithful. The film adds a small line — 'I'm well aware of our bylaws, Severus, having written more than a few myself' — which is consistent with his voice and doesn't distort it.
personality_voice.difference: The film loses some textural detail: the book's Dumbledore is described as having 'fire' in his eyes when defending Hagrid against Fudge (a rare moment of visible passion), and his deliberate precision in confronting Lucius ('speaking very slowly and clearly so that none of them could miss a word') is partially present in the film but slightly softened. The book scene where Dumbledore gives Harry a long, searching look and Harry 'feels as though he is being X-rayed' is compressed. The book Dumbledore explicitly tells Harry that he doesn't think Harry attacked anyone before Harry asks — a subtle leadership gesture — whereas in the film this comes as a direct response to Harry's question. Minor differences only.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main traits, voice patterns, irony, warmth, gravity, and moral authority are preserved. Small losses in internal fire and deliberate staging of confrontations justify a minor deduction but do not meaningfully alter the portrayal.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore in CoS serves several narrative functions: (1) institutional authority who protects Harry and Hagrid from expulsion/punishment; (2) investigator who diagnoses Petrification and reads the Chamber's reopening; (3) loyal advocate who publicly defends Hagrid against Fudge and Malfoy at personal cost; (4) post-crisis anchor who rewards Harry, explains the Parseltongue transfer, delivers the 'choices' moral, confronts Lucius, and enables Dobby's freedom by handing Harry the diary. He is also a background presence whose absence creates dread (the school falls into fear when he is suspended). His agency is active throughout: he initiates, explains, enables, and resolves.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: All major functions are preserved. The film Dumbledore diagnoses Petrification, defends Hagrid against Fudge and Malfoy, is suspended, leaves his coded message to Harry (eyes drifting to Harry under the Invisibility Cloak), returns, conducts the post-crisis debrief, explains Parseltongue, delivers the 'choices' speech, and confronts Lucius with the diary. The Dobby-freeing sequence — Harry asks for the diary and Dumbledore says 'Certainly, Harry. But hurry. The feast, remember' — is preserved intact.
narrative_role_agency.difference: One meaningful reduction: in the book, Dumbledore opens the camera himself and examines the melted film, then delivers the 'Chamber is indeed open again' conclusion as the active investigator. In the film, the camera opens and a jet of steam hisses out, and Dumbledore uses this as evidence for a slightly different line ('our students are in great danger... he would surely be dead'), which changes the register — from measured deduction to more direct alarm. The book's Dumbledore also explicitly frames his post-crisis debrief more theatrically (joking about Lockhart, noting Harry's modesty), all of which is preserved in the film. No major agency transfers to other characters.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The shift in the camera scene slightly reduces Dumbledore's role as calm investigative authority (he becomes more reactive/alarming), but this is minor. All core functions remain intact. Small penalty only.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in CoS are: loyalty to those in his care (Hagrid, Harry, the students); protection of Hogwarts as an institution; and a long-game awareness of Voldemort that others lack. He shows no internal conflict in the conventional sense — his arc in this book is largely flat and intentional. However, there is a subtle tension: he steps aside when suspended not out of weakness but strategic patience ('I will only truly have left this school when none here are loyal to me'), which implies he trusts the institution and Harry more than he forces his own hand. His motivation to give Harry the tools to succeed rather than rescue him directly is implicit throughout (Fawkes, the Sorting Hat).
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves these motivations adequately. His defense of Hagrid, his coded farewell, his post-crisis warmth toward Harry, and his confrontation of Lucius all speak to the same motivational core. The line about only having left when none are loyal is present in the film and clearly aimed at Harry, establishing the same implicit strategy.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film provides less space to see Dumbledore thinking. In the book, he 'peered at Harry' from under his eyebrows after the Parseltongue session, and his gentleness in asking Harry if there is 'anything you'd like to tell me' reveals a deliberate strategy of drawing Harry out rather than interrogating him. The film versions these scenes adequately but slightly more economically. The motivation is the same; the depth of characterisation around it is marginally thinner.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still correct. No change in what Dumbledore wants or why. Minor deduction for reduced texture rather than any alteration.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in CoS is intentionally flat: he begins as trusted headmaster, is removed mid-story, and returns at the end. The 'arc' is structural — his absence makes the threat real; his return signals resolution. He does not change as a person. His consistent characterisation through departure and return is itself the point: he is the stable centre that Hogwarts needs. The closest thing to a development beat is that he trusts Harry enough, after this adventure, to confirm the Parseltongue truth and deliver the 'choices' speech — a moment of deeper confidence-sharing.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows this exactly. Dumbledore is present, removed, and returns. The post-crisis confidence-sharing with Harry is present. No arc is invented or altered.
character_arc.difference: Minimal. The film compresses the post-crisis conversation slightly — the book has more beats (Lockhart's ironic send-off, a longer silence before the Slytherin conversation begins), but nothing structurally important is skipped.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is flat in both and the flat arc is faithfully reproduced. Full score is appropriate but a small deduction for compression of the post-crisis scene's emotional pacing.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dumbledore's key relationships in CoS are: (1) Harry — mentorship with deliberate distance; he draws Harry out, confirms his belonging, gives him tools rather than rescue; (2) Hagrid — fierce, explicit loyalty that costs him politically; (3) Lucius Malfoy — cold, knowing opposition; Dumbledore is never fooled and makes clear he knows exactly what Malfoy has done; (4) McGonagall — trusted lieutenant who executes his will and shares his concern; (5) Fudge — restrained but firm resistance to political pressure.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: All five relationships are represented. The Harry mentor dynamic is intact. The Hagrid loyalty ('I want it understood, Cornelius, that Hagrid has my full confidence') is word-for-word preserved. The Lucius confrontation with the diary — 'one only hopes that no more of Lord Voldemort's old school things find their way into innocent hands' — is present with the same cold precision. McGonagall as trusted lieutenant is functionally intact. The Fudge dynamic is faithfully rendered.
key_relationships.difference: The film slightly compresses the emotional texture of the Harry-Dumbledore relationship. In the book, Dumbledore watches Harry for a long time before speaking after the Chamber events, and the quiet before the 'choices' speech is longer and more charged. The scene where Dumbledore thanks Harry for 'real loyalty' is present but arrives slightly more quickly in the film. These are tonal compressions rather than dynamic changes.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: No relationship is fundamentally altered or reassigned. Minor compression warrants a small penalty.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book Dumbledore has several layers of complexity present in CoS specifically: (1) He is perceptive enough to see through both Harry's lie about the car and Riddle fifty years earlier, but he chooses not to press — strategic restraint rather than ignorance. (2) His 'fire' when defending Hagrid against Fudge is a rare crack in his composure. (3) His coded farewell ('I will only truly have left this school...') is directed at Harry specifically, implying he trusts a twelve-year-old's loyalty in a moment of political crisis — a profound and unusual act. (4) His post-crisis handling of Lockhart ('Impaled upon your own sword, Gilderoy') is dry and pointed. (5) His confrontation of Lucius is a masterclass in saying everything while proving nothing — he lays out the exact mechanism of the plot without making an accusation he cannot prove.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the coded farewell (and makes the eye contact with Harry explicit, which is actually a slight gain in clarity). The Lockhart irony is present. The Lucius confrontation with the diary is present. The fire defending Hagrid is suggested but slightly less marked — the book's specific notation that his eyes held 'a fire Harry had never seen before' is not replicated in the staging.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The most meaningful loss is the book's scene where Dumbledore asks Harry if there is 'anything you'd like to tell me' after the Chamber, and Harry says 'No, sir. Nothing' — the film includes this exchange but at lower stakes, without the weight of Harry knowing that Dumbledore probably knows he's withholding. The book makes Harry's internal conflict ('this is the same sort of no he himself had given Dumbledore') explicit; the film cannot replicate this interiority. Additionally, the book's post-crisis scene includes Dumbledore considering Harry for a long time in silence before beginning — a texture that is largely absent in the film's more efficient transition.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The lost nuances are real but mostly consist of interiority and pacing that film structurally cannot replicate. The key beats of complexity — strategic restraint, dry wit, knowing opposition to Malfoy, trust in Harry — are preserved. The loss of the internal register (Harry recognising himself in Riddle's deflection, Dumbledore seeming to know he's being lied to) reduces the richness without eliminating it. Noticeable simplification but character remains substantially complete.

lost_or_transferred_material: Book description of 'fire in his blue eyes' when defending Hagrid against Fudge — emotional intensity marker that is not replicated in the film staging
Dumbledore's long, charged silence before beginning the post-crisis conversation with Harry — pacing that conveys deliberateness and weight
Harry's internal observation that his own 'No, sir' to Dumbledore was 'the same sort of no' Riddle gave — ironic parallel visible only in book narration
Dumbledore 'speaking very slowly and clearly so that none of them could miss a word' during the suspension scene — book's explicit staging of his calculated precision
Dumbledore proactively telling Harry he doesn't suspect him before Harry asks, rather than in response to Harry's question — a subtle distinction in who controls the scene

Book's explicit notation that Dumbledore's gaze made Harry feel 'as though he were being X-rayed' — a recurring characterisation of his penetrating awareness that is present as description but not as explicit staging in the film
key_observations: The film adaptation of Dumbledore in Chamber of Secrets is substantially faithful. All major functions, relationships, key lines, and characterisation beats are preserved — including the custard tart deflection, the coded farewell under the Invisibility Cloak, the Lockhart irony, the post-crisis 'choices' speech, and the Lucius confrontation. The primary losses are tonal and pacing-related: the book conveys Dumbledore's depth partly through Harry's interiority and through deliberate narrative pauses that film cannot easily replicate. His strategic restraint — knowing more than he reveals, choosing not to press — is visible in both versions but more richly textured in the books. No agency is transferred to other characters and no relationship dynamic is meaningfully altered. The score reflects a highly faithful portrayal with minor deductions for the compression of emotional pacing, the reduced visibility of Dumbledore's rare moments of visible passion, and the structural loss of the internal irony that the book uses to link Harry's behaviour to Riddle's.
